name: Consistency Models
intent: A consistency model is a promise about which values a read may return when data is copied across several machines. Stronger promises are easier to build on but cost speed and availability.
scenario: A user posts a comment. The write goes to the primary database, and read replicas catch up a moment later. The user immediately refreshes the page.
problem: With copies of data on several nodes, a read can land on a node that has not yet received the latest write. The user may not see their own comment, or may see it, refresh, and watch it disappear. Without a stated model, nobody knows which of these surprises are allowed.

howItWorks.title: Strong (linearizable) consistency
howItWorks.text: Every read returns the latest committed write, as if there were a single copy. This is simplest to reason about, but each read or write may have to coordinate with the primary or a quorum, which adds latency and reduces availability during failures.

howItWorks.title: Eventual consistency
howItWorks.text: If no new writes happen, all copies eventually agree. In the meantime a read may return old data, and two reads in a row may even disagree. It is the cheapest and most available model.

howItWorks.title: Read-your-writes
howItWorks.text: A user always sees their own earlier writes, even if others might not see them yet. It is often built by sending that user's reads to the primary, or to a replica known to have caught up, for a short time after they write.

howItWorks.title: Monotonic reads
howItWorks.text: Once a user has seen a value, later reads never show an older one. Time never appears to run backwards. A common way is to keep a user's reads on the same replica.

howItWorks.title: Causal consistency
howItWorks.text: If one event caused another (a reply to a comment), everyone sees them in that order, though unrelated events may appear in different orders for different people. It sits between eventual and strong.

pros: Weaker models give lower latency and higher availability
Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic) fix the most noticeable surprises cheaply
Strong consistency lets application code assume one up-to-date copy
You can choose a different model per operation
cons: Stronger models need coordination, so they are slower and fail more under partitions
Weaker models push complexity onto the application and its users
Bugs from stale reads are intermittent and hard to reproduce
The names are used loosely, so teams often mean different things
whenToUse: Strong for money, inventory, locks, leader election and uniqueness checks
Read-your-writes for anything a user just changed: profiles, settings, posts
Monotonic reads for feeds and dashboards where going backwards looks like a bug
Eventual for counters, recommendations, analytics and caches
whenNotToUse: Do not pay for strong consistency on data that is naturally approximate
Do not use eventual consistency where one user's stale read can cause a harmful action
Do not assume the default setting of a database matches the guarantee your feature needs
pitfalls: A load balancer sending one user's consecutive reads to different replicas
Treating 'eventual' as 'a few milliseconds' when lag can grow under load
Reading from a replica straight after writing, and then acting on the old value
Mixing models in one workflow, so a write goes to one system and the next read comes from another
